title: Why AMC Needs Your Popcorn Money
summary: AMC sends almost half of every ticket back to the movie studios, and the snack bar earns nearly as much as the screen. Plus: why the first cinemas wanted nothing to do with popcorn.
tags: why is movie popcorn so expensive

hooks.hook: In 2025 AMC sold about 219 million movie tickets. Almost half of that ticket money went straight back to the studios.
Why does a bucket of popcorn cost almost as much as the movie?
Cinemas aren't in the movie business. They're in the popcorn business.
This is AMC's 2025 income statement, and the most important line is the snack bar.
The ticket you buy has a silent partner. The popcorn doesn't.

sources: AMC Entertainment Q4 and full-year 2025 results (Form 8-K, Exhibit 99.1, Feb 23, 2026): attendance 219.4M, average ticket $12.09, food & beverage per patron $7.62, admissions $2,652.8M, food & beverage revenue $1,671.3M, film exhibition costs $1,275.2M, food & beverage costs $327.0M, net loss $632.4M: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1411579/000141157926000018/amc-20260223xex99d1.htm

Our calculations from the same release: film costs / admissions = 48.1%; food & beverage costs / food & beverage revenue = 19.6%; per person after direct costs: ticket $12.09 x (1 - 0.481) = $6.28, snacks $7.62 x (1 - 0.196) = $6.13 (before rent and staff).

Cinemark Holdings Q4 and full-year 2025 results (Exhibit 99.1, Feb 18, 2026): admissions $1,544.7M, concession revenue $1,227.2M, film rentals and advertising $877.0M, concession supplies $240.5M (our calculations: 56.8% and 19.6%): https://ir.cinemark.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001193125-26-056010/cnk-ex99_1.htm

AMC Entertainment Q4 and full-year 2019 results (Exhibit 99.1, Feb 27, 2020): attendance 356,443 thousand, average ticket $9.26, food and beverage per patron $4.82: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1411579/000141157920000024/amc-20200227ex991bfe06d.htm

Smithsonian magazine, "Why Do We Eat Popcorn at the Movies?" (Andrew F. Smith quote, 5 to 10 cents a bag, the Dallas chain, over half of US popcorn eaten at theaters by 1945): https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/why-do-we-eat-popcorn-at-the-movies-475063/

scenes.narration: In {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} AMC sold about {219 million|two hundred nineteen million} movie tickets. Almost half of all that ticket money went straight back to the movie studios.
On an average ticket of {$12.09,|twelve dollars and nine cents,} the studios got about {$5.81.|five dollars and eighty-one cents.} That's our math, from AMC's own numbers.

data.title: Average AMC ticket, 2025
data.source: AMC FY2025 results; studios' share = film costs / admissions (our calculation)

scenes.narration: So how does a cinema actually pay its bills? The answer is probably in your hands right now. Buttered.
In the next few minutes: where your ticket money really goes, what the snack bar actually earns, and why the first movie theaters wanted nothing to do with popcorn.
Part one. The ticket is shared.
Across the whole year, AMC paid {$1.28 billion|one point two eight billion dollars} in film costs.
That's about {48 percent|forty-eight percent} of everything it took in at the box office.

data.title: Box office money that went to the studios

scenes.narration: And it isn't just AMC. At Cinemark, another of America's biggest chains, film rentals and advertising took about {57 percent|fifty-seven percent} of ticket sales.

data.title: Ticket money paid out, 2025
data.source: AMC and Cinemark FY2025 results (our calculation: $1,275.2M / $2,652.8M; $877.0M / $1,544.7M)

scenes.narration: And out of the other half, AMC still has to pay for the building, the staff, and the screens.
If you like knowing where your money really goes, subscribe. There's a new breakdown every week.
Part two. The snack bar.
The average AMC customer spent {$7.62|seven dollars and sixty-two cents} on food and drinks.
And here's the twist: the food itself cost AMC only about twenty cents of every dollar.

data.title: Every dollar at the snack bar

scenes.narration: Cinemark's numbers look the same: its snacks also cost it about twenty cents for every dollar you paid.
So per person, the ticket leaves AMC about {$6.28,|six twenty-eight,} and the snacks leave about {$6.13.|six thirteen.}

data.title: Left per person after direct costs
data.source: Before rent and staff. Our calculation from AMC FY2025

scenes.narration: A seven-dollar snack earns almost as much as a twelve-dollar ticket.
For the whole company, snacks were about a third of all revenue, but nearly half of what tickets and snacks earned after their direct costs.

data.title: Snacks' share of ticket + snack earnings
data.source: After film and food costs, before rent and staff (our calculation)

scenes.narration: And the snack bar matters more every year. Since {2019,|twenty nineteen,} AMC's average ticket price went up about {31 percent.|thirty-one percent.} Snack spending per person went up about {58 percent.|fifty-eight percent.}

data.title: AMC, per person: 2019 to 2025
data.source: AMC FY2019 and FY2025 results: ticket $9.26 to $12.09, snacks $4.82 to $7.62 (our calculation)

scenes.narration: That matters, because AMC sold about {137 million|one hundred thirty-seven million} fewer tickets in {2025|twenty twenty-five} than in {2019.|twenty nineteen.} Fewer people, each spending more at the counter.
Part three. The snack nobody wanted.

It wasn't always like this. The first movie palaces copied fancy stage theaters, with beautiful carpets. As food historian Andrew Smith told Smithsonian magazine: movie theaters wanted nothing to do with popcorn.

data.quote: Movie theaters wanted nothing to do with *popcorn.*
data.note: author of Popped Culture, to Smithsonian magazine

scenes.narration: Then came the Great Depression. People wanted cheap fun, and at {5 to 10 cents|five to ten cents} a bag, popcorn was a treat almost anyone could afford.

One Dallas chain put popcorn machines in {80|eighty} of its theaters, but not in its five best ones. Within two years, the theaters with popcorn saw profits soar. The five without it were losing money.
By {1945,|nineteen forty-five,} more than half of all the popcorn eaten in America was eaten at the movies. The snack the theaters didn't want had saved them.
Part four. Why popcorn costs so much.
That's why the snack bar sits right where you walk in, and why the biggest size always looks like the best deal.

lines.text: The big size *looks* like the deal

scenes.narration: It isn't greed hiding in the popcorn. It's math. The ticket has a partner. The popcorn doesn't.
And even with all that popcorn, AMC still reported a net loss of {$632 million|six hundred thirty-two million dollars} in {2025.|twenty twenty-five.}
Without the snack bar's one point three billion dollars in earnings, that hole would be far deeper.

Ninety years ago, popcorn helped cinemas survive the Depression. Today it's still doing the same job. So next time the popcorn feels expensive, remember: you're not just buying a snack. You're helping keep the lights on. Next: another everyday price, taken apart.
